extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, researchers, and others interested in publication integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying, diagnosing, and responding to compromised peer review in journal publishing — including detection of red flags, editorial safeguards to prevent manipulation, and corrective actions such as retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised peer review → retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Following an investigation by the publisher, the parties have concluded that this article was accepted solely on the basis of a compromised peer review process. Therefore, the article must be retracted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an investigation concludes an article was accepted solely because the peer review process was compromised, retraction is the indicated corrective action. Retraction notices should state the finding and the resulting action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify concerning peer review patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher had “identified concerning peer review patterns associated with manuscripts in progress as well as some previously published papers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor for anomalous patterns across submissions and published items (e.g., clusters of related manuscripts, similar reviewer activity, repeated quick acceptances). Investigate batches rather than only single papers when patterns emerge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non‑institutional or random email addresses as a red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: “Most of the corresponding authors had email domains not associated with a university or research organization, containing random sequences of letters and numbers, a potential sign of paper mill activity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat non‑institutional email domains and addresses with random strings as suspicious; incorporate email-domain checks into screening and reviewer verification processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper mill indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomized/non-institutional emails and other recurring anomalies can be a “potential sign of paper mill activity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider multiple indicators (contact info, similarity across manuscripts, unusual authorship patterns) together to flag possible paper-mill submissions and trigger further scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor responsibility and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may claim they “were not involved in the peer review process. ‘This is the editor’s responsibility,’” placing responsibility for integrity with editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are responsible for the integrity of peer review processes (selection/verification of reviewers, oversight of review outcomes). Editorial workflows should make responsibilities and checks explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk from accepting author‑suggested reviewers without verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters point out manipulation “usually happens with authors who know the editor in chief and give him unofficially the name of reviewers real or fake” or when editors accept suggested reviewers without checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept author‑suggested reviewers blindly; verify reviewer identities, affiliations, and contact information independently of details supplied by authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer identity verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulation can occur via fake reviewer names/emails; reviewers should be vetted rather than assumed genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement procedures to verify reviewer identity (institutional email, ORCID, prior publications, independent contact verification) before relying on their reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit and monitor guest editor powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Guest editors can be a vulnerability: their role may enable manipulation if not limited (“The guest editor’s role was basically to suggest potential authors and encourage them to submit...”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit guest editors’ unilateral decision-making power, clearly define their responsibilities, and apply additional oversight for guest‑edited issues (e.g., editorial-board signoff, audit of chosen reviewers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer thoroughness and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Substandard peer review — “the reviewers not doing their job properly” — contributes to low-quality or ‘garbage’ articles getting through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reviewer reports for depth and rigor; prefer reviewers with demonstrated expertise and require substantive critiques. Use editorial judgment to detect perfunctory or superficial reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher monitoring and corrective action (transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers (e.g., Wiley, Hindawi) monitor, investigate, and may perform mass retractions; retraction notices often state agreement between the journal Editor‑in‑Chief and publisher and sometimes note author disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should proactively monitor for anomalies, conduct investigations, and act (including batch retractions) when warranted. Retraction notices should be transparent about reasons and indicate if authors disagree.
